criterion_notes.c1: Examines piped drinking-water supply service access, household connections, exclusion, and service continuity in the small town of Moamba, Mozambique (zooming in on Bairro Central and Block Q11).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines water governance, decentralization of authority, and socio-political power dynamics in piped water provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although framed theoretically around 'sociotechnical tinkering' across design, construction, operation, and use, the paper empirically analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access: (1) cost-recovery and upfront connection-fee rules (the private concession utility requiring Block Q11 residents to pay full material costs for network extension; the block chief enforcing a 50 MT contribution rule for initial connection and a 500 MT late-entry fee rule, prohibiting non-paying households from connecting); (2) utility discretion and accommodation toward unauthorized user-built extensions (connecting the unauthorized recycled pipeline to the main branch and signing formal client contracts with monthly billing, while refusing maintenance responsibility on the ground that the pipe is not utility property and conditioning leak repair on user contributions of labor and materials); (3) street-level operator discretion over rotational rationing schedules and extended supply hours; and (4) plural/informal hydraulic property rules governing water entitlements.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative ethnographic empirical case study drawing on two fieldwork periods (November 2017–February 2018 and January–March 2019), systematic infrastructure and practice observations, comparison of engineering design maps and satellite imagery, and 47 in-depth semi-structured interviews (4 local authority staff, 9 water utility workers including the general manager, 2 construction workers, and 32 water users in Bairro Central). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are explicitly eligible for the systematic review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access outcomes including private household piped connection vs. prohibition/exclusion of poorer non-contributing households (who must buy water from connected neighbors or seek water elsewhere), service intermittency and duration (e.g., 5-hour daily rotational schedule, 4-day, 5-day, and 15-day supply interruptions, water pressure), and billing complaints from air-induced false meter readings.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (Moamba's piped water distribution network and households/actors in Bairro Central and Block Q11; n=47 interviewees including 32 neighborhood water users), exposure (utility cost-recovery/extension rules, accommodation of unauthorized pipelines, contested infrastructure property/maintenance rules, community connection-fee rules, and operator rationing discretion), outcome (household connection, exclusion, and service continuity/reliability), and study design (qualitative ethnographic case study) are all clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: The work presented in this paper is based on a detailed qualitative study of the piped water system in Moamba, a small town located 62.5 km from Maputo, Mozambique. Four months of ﬁeldwork were carried out between November 2017 and February 2018 with a follow-up ﬁeldwork period from January to March 2019.

Systematic observations of the water infrastructure and its functioning, as well as the everyday practices of operators and water users, were cross-checked with data collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews conducted with 47 actors.

Those households that refused or could not aﬀord to pay for the installation costs were prohibited from installing private household connections to the pipe. Nowadays, households who wish to be connected to the pipe but who did not contribute to the installation of the pipe have to pay 500 MT.

In this way, the installation of the recycled pipeline created new rules that divided the neighborhood between households who have the right to use the water from the self-installed pipe and those who do not have this entitlement. Those excluded—and often poorer—households have to buy water from households that are connected to the pipe, leaving them on the mercy of their neighbors, or search of water elsewhere.

They argued that because the pipe was not the property of the water utility, they needed permission from the collective of water users to intervene in this part of the system (IN37, IN33, IN47). Taking into account the water users connected to this pipe are nowadays formal clients of the utility with signed contracts and monthly payments of the water bills, it could be argued that, in order to better serve its clients, it might be reasonable for the water utility to replace the self-installed pipe entirely with a brand new pipe.
As a condition to repair the pipe, the water utility demanded investment labor and materials from the water users as proof of their commitment to keep the infrastructure in a good state.

raw_response.exposure: Sociotechnical tinkering and rule-type access mechanisms: utility network-extension cost-recovery requirements, utility discretion/accommodation toward unauthorized resident-built pipelines, contested pipe ownership and conditional maintenance/shutoff rules, local connection-fee/hydraulic property rules (50 MT initial vs. 500 MT late-entry fee), and street-level operator discretion over rotational rationing schedules.
raw_response.outcome: Household piped water connection vs. exclusion of non-paying poorer households (reliance on neighbor water resale or alternative sources), service continuity/intermittency and supply hours, water pressure, and air-induced false meter billing.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Piped water treatment and distribution network in Moamba, Mozambique (concession area ~24,650 inhabitants), zooming in on Bairro Central and Block Q11 (Quarteirao 11); 47 semi-structured interviewees (4 local authority staff, 9 water utility workers including general manager, 2 construction workers, and 32 water users in Bairro Central).
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative ethnographic case study in Moamba, Mozambique meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type readings of Criterion 2. Beyond its broader sociotechnical tinkering framework, it empirically documents concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing household piped water access and continuity—including utility cost-recovery barriers to network extension, utility accommodation of an unauthorized user-installed pipeline paired with formal billing contracts yet contested pipe ownership during shutoffs/repairs, conditional user labor/material requirements for repairs, community-enforced upfront and late-comer connection fee rules (50 MT vs. 500 MT) that exclude poorer households from private connections, and operator discretion over rotational rationing schedules. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with identifiable population, exposure, outcome, and design are included for the mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative ethnographic case study (in-depth semi-structured interviews, systematic field observations, engineering design document review, and satellite image comparison)
